questions.q: How does measurement standard error scale with shot count, and what does that mean for halving the error?
options: Standard error scales as 1/sqrt(shots), so halving the error requires 4x the shots, not 2x
Standard error scales linearly with shots, so halving the error requires exactly 2x the shots
Standard error is independent of shot count
Standard error scales as shots^2, so halving the error requires only a 41% increase in shots
questions.explain: Since standard error is proportional to 1/sqrt(shots), reducing it by half requires the shot count to increase by a factor of 2^2 = 4, as shown going from 1,000 to 4,000 shots (0.0316 -> 0.0158).

questions.q: In the Rigetti Ankaa-3 example, going from 1,000 to 4,000 shots per task across 200 tasks increases cost from $240.00 to $780.00 -- a 3.25x increase. Why isn't this increase exactly 4x, matching the shot multiplier?
options: The flat $0.30 per-task fee doesn't scale with shots, so only the per-shot cost (which does scale 4x) drives most, but not all, of the total cost increase
AWS Braket gives a volume discount on shots above 1,000
The per-shot fee actually decreases as shot count per task increases
The calculation in the lesson is an approximation with no real explanation
questions.explain: The per-task fee ($60 total either way) stays fixed while per-shot cost ($180 -> $720, exactly 4x) grows with shots, so the blended total increase (3.25x) falls short of a clean 4x because of the fixed per-task component.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the correct basis for setting a shot budget, rather than picking a 'thorough-sounding' round number like 10,000 shots?
options: The precision actually required by the downstream decision the result feeds into -- e.g., whether a threshold crossing needs to be resolved to within 0.05 or 0.01
Always use the maximum shot count the provider allows, regardless of cost
Match whatever shot count a research paper used, regardless of your own use case
Shot count should always be set to exactly 1,000, since that's the industry default
questions.explain: The lesson frames shot-budget sizing as an application question -- what precision does the downstream decision actually require -- not an arbitrary 'more is always better' or round-number choice.

questions.q: The lesson computes that padding a 200-task job's shot count from 2,500 to 10,000 shots per task costs an extra $1,350 on Ankaa-3 pricing. What is this extra cost paying for, according to the lesson's argument?
options: Precision beyond what the use case's own decision threshold requires -- effectively wasted spend if the downstream decision doesn't change at that higher precision level
A mandatory provider fee for high-shot-count jobs
Faster execution time on the QPU
A reduction in queue wait time
questions.explain: The lesson's core argument is that shot padding 'for safety' has a real, computable dollar cost, and that cost is only justified if the extra precision actually changes a downstream decision -- otherwise it's money spent on precision nobody needed.

questions.q: A use case needs a standard error of 0.015 or better, given 1,000 shots yields 0.0316. Approximately how many shots are needed to meet this target?
options: About 4,450 shots, computed as 1,000 x (0.0316/0.015)^2
About 500 shots, since fewer shots always means less noise
Exactly 2,000 shots, since that's double the baseline
1,000 shots is already sufficient, since 0.0316 rounds to 0.015
questions.explain: Since standard error scales as 1/sqrt(shots), shots needed = 1,000 x (0.0316/0.015)^2 ~= 1,000 x 4.45 ~= 4,450 shots to bring standard error down to about 0.015.
